lead: Isaiah looks at a felled royal house and sees one green shoot, on whom the Spirit of the Lord will rest, and around whom creation itself will be at peace. In Luke that future arrives: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and tells his disciples that their eyes are seeing what prophets and kings longed to see. The first reading is the longing of Advent; the Gospel says the waiting has not been in vain.

r.h: A shoot from the stump of Jesse
set: Isaiah prophesied in Judah in the eighth century BC, when Assyria was swallowing the small kingdoms around it and the kings of David's line were often a disappointment. Chapter 10 has just ended with the image of a great forest cut down by the Lord. Chapter 11 begins with what grows after the axe: hope comes where everything looks finished.
str: v. 1: the shoot and the branch.
vv. 2–3a: the Spirit who rests on him.
vv. 3b–5: his justice, above all for the poor.
vv. 6–9: peace among the animals and on the holy mountain.
v. 10: the root of Jesse as a signal to the nations.
kw: What remains of a felled tree. Isaiah says the stump of Jesse, not of David. God goes back behind the palace to the shepherd family of Bethlehem and begins again.
A green shoot. Many interpreters hear this word behind Matthew's saying that Jesus “will be called a Nazorean” (Matthew 2:23), though Matthew does not explain it.
The same word means breath and wind. The king's power will not be his own army but the breath of God resting on him.
vv: A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots.
God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7) survives the failure of David's sons. The stump looks dead, but the root is alive.
The spirit of the Lord shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord.
The Hebrew names six gifts, and “fear of the Lord” comes again in v. 3. The Greek and Latin versions render the first “fear” as “piety”, and so the Church came to count seven gifts.
The wolf shall live with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the kid

This is poetry about a world healed at its root, with the harmony of Eden restored. The reason follows in v. 9: the earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord. Where God is known, no one needs to hurt anyone.
ch: The Catechism sees in these verses the features of the promised Messiah, on whom the Spirit rests (CCC 712), and draws from them its teaching on the seven gifts, which “belong in their fullness to Christ, Son of David” (CCC 1831). St Paul quotes v. 10 to show that the nations too hope in Christ (Romans 15:12). St Jerome, playing on the Latin virga (shoot) and virgo (virgin), took the shoot as Mary and the flower that rises from it as Christ (in substance).

set: The disciples have just come back from their mission full of joy (10:17–20). Jesus tells them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven. Then he himself rejoices. Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 11:25–27), but only Luke tells us of the joy and of the Holy Spirit.
str: v. 21: Jesus' prayer of thanks to the Father.
v. 22: the unique knowledge between the Father and the Son.
vv. 23–24: a private blessing on the disciples.
kw: A strong word for exultant, festive joy. Luke uses it of Mary's spirit in the Magnificat (1:47). Here the joy of Jesus is the joy of the Holy Spirit.
Little ones who cannot yet speak well. They are the disciples, simple people who receive what the learned refuse. Jesus is not praising ignorance, but the open hand.
vv: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants
The whole Trinity appears in one verse: the Son rejoices in the Holy Spirit and gives thanks to the Father. The shoot of Isaiah, on whom the Spirit rests, is praying.
no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.
To “know” here means a shared life and not only information. We know the Father only because the Son lets us into what he himself has with the Father.
Blessed are the eyes that see what you see!
The prophets, Isaiah among them, saw from far away (compare Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 1:10–12). The disciples are looking at the promise itself.
ch: The Catechism counts this among the two explicit prayers of Jesus preserved from his public ministry, and notes that each begins with thanksgiving (CCC 2603). It also cites the parallel in Matthew when it teaches that Jesus revealed God as Father in an unheard-of sense (CCC 240). The Church's Advent is a school for such little ones: the Lord who came is known by those who receive him as a gift.

qa: Are there six gifts of the Holy Spirit in Isaiah, or seven?

The Hebrew text of 11:2–3 names six and mentions the fear of the Lord twice. The Greek and Latin translations gave the first mention as “piety”, which gives seven. The Church's list of seven (CCC 1831) rests on that long reading of the text. Seven also suggests fullness, which is the point: the Spirit rests on the Messiah without measure, and we share his gifts.
study: Where in my life or my family does the stump look dead? What would it mean to look there for a shoot?
Jesus thanks the Father for revealing himself to “infants”. What keeps me from receiving God's word like one of them?
